passages.source_text: ἐμοῦ δὲ εἰπόντος Ἤθελόν τινι συντυχεῖν τῶν ἑορακότων αὐτόν, εὐθὺς ἦγόν με λέγοντες Ἔστιν τις ἐνταῦθα οὐ μόνον ἱστορήσας αὐτὸν ἀλλὰ καὶ τῆς ἐκεῖθεν γῆς ὑπάρχων, ἀνὴρ Ἑβραῖος, ὀνόματι Βαρνάβας, ὃς καὶ ἕνα τῶν αὐτοῦ μαθητῶν ἑαυτὸν εἶναι λέγει καὶ ἐνταῦθά που καθεζόμενος τῆς ἐκείνου ὑποσχέσεως τοὺς λόγους τοῖς βουλομένοις ἑτοίμως λέγει. καὶ δὴ συνῆλθον αὐτοῖς. καὶ ἐλθών, σὺν τῷ παρεστῶτι ὄχλῳ ἔστην ἐπακούων τῶν λόγων, καὶ συνενόουν τἀληθῆ οὐ διαλεκτικῇ τέχνῃ λέγοντα, ἀλλὰ ἀκάκως καὶ ἀπαρασκευάστως ἐκτιθέμενον ἅ τε ἤκουσεν καὶ ἑόρακεν τὸν τοῦ θεοῦ φανέντα υἱὸν πεποιηκέναι τε καὶ εἰρηκέναι· πολλοὺς δὲ μάρτυρας τῶν ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ λεγομένων θαυμασίων τε καὶ λόγων καὶ ἐξ αὐτοῦ τοῦ παρεστῶτος ὄχλου παρεῖχεν.

ἐπειδὴ δὲ πρὸς τὰ ἀπανούργως λεγόμενα· ἡδέως οἱ ὄχλοι διετίθεντο, οἱ ἐκ παιδείας κοσμικῆς ὁρμώμενοι φιλόσοφοι γελᾶν αὐτὸν καὶ χλευάζειν ἐπεβάλλοντο, σκώπτοντες καὶ διασύροντες θράσει ἀμέτρῳ, ὡς μεγάλοις ὅπλοις κεχρημένοι τοῖς συλλογισμοῖς. ὁ δὲ ἀπωθούμενος αὐτῶν τὸν λῆρον οὐ συνέτρεχεν αὐτῶν τῇ πανούργῳ πεύσει, ἀλλ᾽ ἀκαταπλήκτως ὢν ἔλεγεν οὐκ ἀφίστατο. καὶ ποτέ τις αὐτοῦ ἐπύθετο διὰ τί κώνωψ ἐγένετο καὶ βραχύτατον ὄν, ἓξ πόδας ἔχον ἔχει καὶ πτερά, ἐλέφας δέ, τὸ μέγιστον τῶν ζῴων, ἄπτερος ὢν τέσσαρας μόνους ἔχει πόδας. ὁ δὲ μετὰ τὴν πεῦσιν τὸν ἐμποδισθέντα ἀναλαβὼν λόγον, ὡς πρὸς τὴν πεῦσιν ἀποκρινάμενος τὸν αὐτῷ ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς προκείμενον ἀνελάμβανεν λόγον τούτῳ μόνῳ προοιμίῳ χρώμενος καθ᾽ ἑκάστην ἐνκοπὴν Ἡμεῖς τοῦ πέμψαντος ἡμᾶς τοὺς λόγους καὶ τὰς θαυμασίους πράξεις εἰπεῖν ὑμῖν μόνον ἔχομεν ἐντολήν, καὶ ἀντὶ τῆς λογικῆς ἀποδείξεως μάρτυρας παρέχομεν ὑμῖν τῶν ἐξ ὑμῶν παρεστώτων πολλούς, ὧν ἐγὼ τὰ εἴδη μέμνημαι ὡς ἐμψύχους εἰκόνας ἱκανὰς μαρτυρίας. λοιπὸν τῆς ὑμετέρας ἐστὶν ἐξουσίας ὑπείκειν ἢ ἀπειθεῖν. τοῦ δὲ λέγειν ὑμῖν τὸ συμφέρον οὐ παύσομαι, ὅτι ἐμοὶ μὲν ζημία τὸ σιωπᾶν, ὑμῖν δὲ τὸ ἀπειθεῖν βλάβη. ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν εἰκαίων ὑμῶν προβλημάτων τὰς ἀποδείξεις ἀποδοῦναι ἐδυνάμην, εἰ φιλαλήθως ἐπυνθάνεσθε. κώνωπος δὲ καὶ ἐλέφαντος τὴν αἰτίαν τῆς διαφόρου δημιουργίας νῦν ὑμῖν εἰπεῖν οὐκ ἔστιν εὔκαιρον τοῖς τῶν ὅλων ἀγνοοῦσι θεόν.

ταῦτα αὐτοῦ λέγοντος, ὡς ἐκ συμφωνίας ἄτακτον ἠφίεσαν γέλωτα, κατασιωπᾶν καὶ ἀπορεῖν αὐτὸν πειρώμενοι ὡς βάρβαρόν τινα δαιμονῶντα. ἐγὼ δὲ ταῦτα ὁρῶν, ζήλῳ οὐκ οἶδ’ ὅπως ληφθεὶς εὐσεβεῖ θυμῷ τοῦ λοιποῦ σιγᾶν οὐκ ἐκαρτέρουν, ἀλλὰ μετὰ παρρησίας ἐβόων λέγων Εὐλόγως ὁ θεὸς ὑμῖν ἀκατάληπτον τὴν αὐτοῦ βούλησιν ἔθετο, ἀναξίους προιδὼν ὡς ἐξ ὧν νῦν τοὺς κριτικὸν νοῦν ἔχοντας πληροφορῶν φαίνεται. ἐπεὶ γὰρ νῦν τῆς αὐτοῦ βουλήσεως κήρυκες ἐξαπεστάλησαν, οὐ γραμματικὴν ἐπαγγελλόμενοι τέχνην, ἀλλὰ ἁπλοῖς καὶ ἀπανούργοις λόγοις τὴν αὐτοῦ βούλησιν ἐκφαίνοντες, ὡς πάνθ’ ὁντιναοῦν ἀκούσαντα νοεῖν τὰ λεγόμενα, καὶ οὐ μετὰ ξέσεώς τινος φθονερᾶς, παρέχειν πᾶσιν ἑαυτὴν μὴ βουλομένης: πάρεστε ὑμεῖς πρὸς τῷ μὴ νοεῖν τὸ ὑμῖν συμφέρον ἐπὶ τῇ ὑμετέρᾳ βλάβῃ γελᾶν τὴν εἰς τὴν ὑμετέραν καταδίκην ἐν βαρβάροις πολιτευσαμένην ἀλήθειαν, ἣν καὶ ὑμῖν ἐπιδημήσασαν ξενίσαι οὐ βούλεσθε διὰ τὰς ἀσελγείας ὑμῶν καὶ τὸ λιτὸν τῶν λόγων αὐτῆς, ἵνα μὴ ἐλεγχθῆτε ὅτι εἰκῇ φιλόλογοί ἐστε καὶ οὐ φιλαληθεῖς φιλόσοφοι. μέχρι μὲν οὖν πότε λαλεῖν μανθάνετε οἱ τὸ καλῶς λαλεῖν οὐκ ἔχοντες; πολλὰ γὰρ παρ’ ὑμῶν ῥήματα ἑνὸς οὐκ ἄξια λόγου. τί ἄρα ἐρεῖ ὑμῶν τὸ ἑλληνικὸν πλῆθος μία ψυχὴ γενόμενον, εἴπερ ἔσται κρίσις, ὡς οὗτος λέγει; Διὰ τί, ὦ θεέ, τὴν σὴν βούλησιν οὐκ ἐκήρυξας ἡμῖν; οὐ πάντως ἀκούσεσθε (εἴπερ ἀποκρίσεως καταξιωθήσεσθε) τάδε Ἐγὼ πάσας τὰς ἐσομένας πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου εἰδὼς προαιρέσεις, ἑκάστῳ πρὸς τὸ αὐτοῦ ἄξιον λανθανόντως προαπήντησα· τοῦτο δὲ αὐτὸ ὅτι οὕτως ἔχει βουληθεὶς τοὺς προσπεφευγότας μοι πληροφορήσαι διὰ τί ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ἐκ προτέρων γενεῶν τὴν ἐμὴν βούλησιν δημοσίᾳ οὐκ εἴασα κηρυχθῆναι, νῦν πρὸς τῷ τέλει τοῦ βίου κήρυκας ἐμῆς βουλῆς ἀπέστειλα, οἳ καὶ γελῶνται καὶ ὑβριζόμενοι χλευάζονται ὑπὸ τῶν μηδὲν ὠφελεῖσθαι θελόντων καὶ ἐπιτεταμένως τὴν ἐμὴν φιλίαν παραιτησαμένων. ὢ μεγάλης ἀδικίας· μέχρι φόνου κινδυνεύουσιν κήρυκες, καὶ ταῦτα ὑπὸ τῶν εἰς σωτηρίαν καλουμένων ἀνδρῶν.

τοῦτο δὲ τὸ ἀδίκως γινόμενον κατὰ τῶν ἐμῶν κηρύκων ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ἂν εἰς πάντας ἐγίνετο, εἴπερ ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς εἰς σωτηρίαν ἐκαλοῦντο οἱ ἀνάξιοι. τὸ γὰρ νῦν γινόμενον ὑπ’ αὐτῶν ἀδίκως εἰς ἀπολογίαν τῆς ἐμῆς δικαίας γίνεται προνοίας, ὅτι καλῶς τὸν τιμῆς ἄξιον λόγον ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς δημοσίᾳ εἰς ὕβριν θεῖναι οὐκ ἐβουλήθην ἀνωφελῶς, ἀλλὰ σιγᾶσθαι αὐτὸν ὡς τίμιον ἐβουλευσάμην, οὐκ ἀπὸ τῶν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ἀξίων (οἷς καὶ μετέδωκα), ἀλλὰ ἀπὸ τούτων καὶ τῶν τοιούτων (ὡς ὁρᾶτε) ἀναξίων, τῶν ἐμὲ μισούντων καὶ ἑαυτοὺς φιλεῖν μὴ βουλομένων. καὶ νῦν γε παρέντες· γελᾶν τὸν ἄνδρα τοῦτον ἐμοῦ πρὸς τὸ τούτου ἐπάγγελμα πυνθάνεσθε ἢ πυνθανομένῳ μοι ὁ βουλόμενος ἀποκρινάσθω, καὶ μὴ ὡς ἀσελγεῖς κύνες ὑλάσσετε, ψόφῳ ἀτάκτῳ μύοντες τῶν σώζεσθαι θελόντων τὰς ἀκοάς. ἄδικοι καὶ θεοστυγεῖς καὶ τὸν σώζοντα λογισμὸν εἰς ἀπιστίαν ἀπασχολοῦντες, πῶς συγγνώμης τυχεῖν δυνήσεσθε, τὸν τὴν θειότητα τοῦ θεοῦ ἐπαγγελλόμενον ὑμῖν εἰπεῖν ὑβρίζοντες, καὶ ταῦτα ἄνθρωπον ὃν ἐχρῆν εἰ καὶ μηδὲν ἀληθὲς λέγοντα διὰ τὴν ἀγαθὴν αὐτοῦ πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἀποδέξασθαι προαίρεσιν;

context.translation_policy_text:
# Translation Stance

This document states the translation commitments that guide every
decision in the People's Open Bible. Declaring them is an act of
honesty: critics can assess our output against our stated
commitments rather than guessing at hidden biases.

> **Status: first draft.** This document will be refined as the
> project matures. Input and disagreement are welcomed via GitHub
> issues.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω
and **phileo-love** for φιλέω, including the repeated question in verse 17.
The ἀγάπη noun's general table entry below is not a rule erasing that verb
pattern. Do not revert this approved POB/SPOB wording to generic “love”.

## Contested terms

The following terms appear frequently and carry heavy theological
weight. Our default rendering and rationale are recorded here.
Per-verse variance is documented in the individual YAML files.

| Greek / Hebrew | Default English | Alternatives considered | Rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Χριστός *Christos* | Messiah where independently titular; Christ in the name forms "Jesus Christ" / "Christ Jesus" | Christ, Messiah | Preserves the title's Hebraic messianic meaning while using the recognizable conventional English personal name |
| κύριος *Kyrios* | Lord | LORD, Master | Matches covenantal and NT usage |
| δοῦλος *doulos* | servant | bondservant, slave | Uses reader-facing "servant" consistently; documents bonded-status and ownership nuance in notes/audit metadata |
| πίστις *pistis* | faith | faithfulness, trust | Main text: faith; footnote alternatives where contested |
| δικαιοσύνη *dikaiosynē* | righteousness | justice | Both renderings preserved in footnotes for Pauline passages |
| ἱλαστήριον *hilastērion* | atoning sacrifice | propitiation, mercy seat | Dynamic rendering for accessibility; alternatives footnoted |
| ἀγάπη *agapē* | love | charity (archaic) | Lexical cognates in source kept |
| σάρξ *sarx* | flesh (literal) / sinful nature (metaphorical) | — | Context-dependent; per-verse documented |
| μετανοέω / μετάνοια *metanoeō / metanoia* | reorient / reorientation; toward God where the context warrants making the destination explicit | repent / repentance (traditional); reconsider / change of mind in documented exceptions | See "Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)" below; do not homogenize regret, divine relenting, or distinct turning words |
| νήφω *nēphō* | clear-minded (most contexts); sober (where Paul explicitly runs the drunk/sober metaphor) | sober-minded | See revision notes in 1 Pet 5:8, 1 Thess 5:6 |
| יְהוָה YHWH | Yahweh | the LORD, Jehovah | Renders the divine name as a name. Where the NT quotes an OT YHWH passage using *Kyrios*, the NT verse retains "Lord" to preserve the Greek; the OT source verse uses "Yahweh". |
| אָדָם *adam* | man / humankind (context) | — | Context-dependent per usage |

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.

## Change log for this document

Material changes to this document are themselves commits. Prior
versions of the stance are preserved in git history.

- **2026-04-21:** Removed creedal affirmations (Apostles' Creed,
  Nicene Creed, Chalcedonian Definition) and replaced with a
  theological-stance section that declines specific creedal
  commitment. Translation philosophy and contested-terms table
  preserved unchanged; those are methodology, not creedal
  commitment, and the project actually runs on them. Added a
  "Translating into other languages" section stating POB's long-
  term intention to ship in every feasible major language, with
  the full revision pipeline and transparent supported-language
  disclosure. Per-verse YAML citing the old `doctrine_reference`
  values is preserved as historical record; those are not
  retroactively edited.
context.ambiguity_review_standard: Apply the supplied DOCTRINE.md ambiguity policy: a defensible contextual rendering may be used in the main text when material alternatives and the reason for the choice are preserved in notes. A unique or uncontested interpretation is not required. Distinguish (a) an unreadable or unverified source, omitted content, invented restoration, or a construction for which no defensible English can be given, from (b) ordinary lexical, attachment, or referent ambiguity faithfully preserved in English or explained with viable alternatives. The former blocks publication; the latter does not automatically block it. A note cannot excuse unsupported wording: the proposed main rendering must itself be defensible from the supplied Greek. Clearly printed gaps must remain gaps, not be filled by invention. Never change a verdict merely to achieve acceptance.

passages.text: When I said, “I would like to meet someone among those who had seen him,” they immediately led me away, saying, “There is someone here who has not only become personally acquainted with him but is also from the land there—a Hebrew man named Barnabas. He also says that he is one of his disciples, and, sitting somewhere around here, he readily tells those who wish to hear the words of that man’s promise.” So I went along with them. When I arrived, I stood with the crowd that was present, listening to his words, and I realized that he was speaking the truth, not by dialectical skill, but was setting out without guile and without preparation both what he had heard and what he had seen the Son of God who had appeared do and say. He also supplied, from the very crowd then present, many witnesses for both the wonders and the words he was recounting.

lexical_decisions.chosen: I would like to meet someone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The imperfect ἤθελον can express a polite or tentative desire; “I wanted to meet” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: who has not only become personally acquainted with him
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἱστορέω with a person can mean visiting or gaining firsthand acquaintance, not merely collecting information. “Who has visited him” or “who has investigated him” are possible but less responsive to Clement’s request to meet an eyewitness.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the words of that man’s promise
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπόσχεσις denotes a promise or undertaking. The demonstrative is retained rather than replaced with a named referent.

lexical_decisions.chosen: without guile and without preparation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering preserves both Barnabas’s lack of deceit or artifice and the extemporaneous character of his presentation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the Son of God who had appeared
lexical_decisions.rationale: φανέντα describes the Son as having appeared or become manifest; the wording does not itself specify how that appearance is to be understood.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῶν ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ λεγομένων θαυμασίων τε καὶ λόγων
lexical_decisions.chosen: for both the wonders and the words he was recounting
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive identifies what the witnesses attest. αὐτοῦ most naturally refers to Barnabas as the one recounting them, though the words and wonders themselves concern the appeared Son.

source_issues.issue: This is a non-Attic or later perfect form of ὁράω rather than the classical-looking ἑωρακότων. The same passage later prints ἑόρακεν, supporting an orthographic pattern rather than an unreadable source. The meaning is secure, and the printed form is not emended in the translation.

passages.text: But because the crowds were favorably disposed toward what was being said without guile, the philosophers who came from a worldly education began laughing at him and jeering at him, making jokes and deriding him with immeasurable insolence, as though they were wielding syllogisms as mighty weapons. He, however, thrust aside their nonsense and did not join in their crafty questioning; instead, undaunted, he continued speaking without stopping. Once someone asked him why a gnat came into being and, though extremely small, has six feet and also wings, whereas the elephant, the largest of animals, though wingless, has only four feet. After the question, he took up the discourse that had been interrupted. As his answer to the question, he resumed the discourse that had been before him from the beginning, using only the following preface after each interruption: “We have been commanded only to tell you the words and marvelous deeds of the one who sent us. Instead of a logical demonstration, we offer you many witnesses from among you who are present, whose faces I remember as living images and sufficient testimonies. From this point it is within your power to yield or to disobey. But I will not cease telling you what benefits you, because silence is loss to me, while disobedience is harm to you. I could also supply demonstrations in answer to your groundless challenges, if you were asking with love for truth. But it is not timely now to tell you, who are ignorant of the God of all things, the reason for the differing creation of the gnat and the elephant.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πρὸς τὰ ἀπανούργως λεγόμενα· ἡδέως οἱ ὄχλοι διετίθεντο
lexical_decisions.chosen: the crowds were favorably disposed toward what was being said without guile
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἡδέως διετίθεντο describes a favorable or pleased response, while ἀπανούργως emphasizes the absence of craftiness.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ συνέτρεχεν αὐτῶν τῇ πανούργῳ πεύσει
lexical_decisions.chosen: did not join in their crafty questioning
lexical_decisions.rationale: The literal image is that he did not “run together with” their questioning. The English expresses his refusal to follow them into their contrived line of inquiry.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he took up the discourse that had been interrupted
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐμποδίζω here describes the discourse as impeded by the question, and ἀναλαμβάνω marks its resumption.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὧν ἐγὼ τὰ εἴδη μέμνημαι ὡς ἐμψύχους εἰκόνας ἱκανὰς μαρτυρίας
lexical_decisions.chosen: whose faces I remember as living images and sufficient testimonies
lexical_decisions.rationale: εἴδη can mean forms, appearances, or faces. “Faces” suits remembered eyewitnesses; “whose forms I remember” remains possible. The appositional language treats those remembered appearances as living images and adequate testimony.

lexical_decisions.chosen: your groundless challenges
lexical_decisions.rationale: εἰκαῖος can describe what is random, purposeless, or without sound basis, while προβλήματα are questions or challenges put forward. “Your random questions” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you, who are ignorant of the God of all things
lexical_decisions.rationale: τῶν ὅλων belongs with θεόν and identifies God as God of the totality, not merely as a god unknown in some limited respect.

source_issues.source_quote: ἐπειδὴ δὲ πρὸς τὰ ἀπανούργως λεγόμενα· ἡδέως οἱ ὄχλοι διετίθεντο
source_issues.issue: The printed middle point after λεγόμενα interrupts the ἐπειδή clause even though ἡδέως οἱ ὄχλοι διετίθεντο supplies its finite verb. This appears to be editorial punctuation rather than missing wording, and the translation construes the clause continuously.
source_issues.proposed_reading: ἐπειδὴ δὲ πρὸς τὰ ἀπανούργως λεγόμενα ἡδέως οἱ ὄχλοι διετίθεντο,

passages.text: As he was saying these things, they let loose disorderly laughter as though by common agreement, trying to silence him and leave him at a loss, as though he were some raving barbarian. When I saw this, I was seized—I do not know how—with zeal and pious indignation. I could no longer endure remaining silent, but cried out boldly, saying: “With good reason God has made his will incomprehensible to you, foreseeing that you were unworthy, as is now evident from the very things by which he fully convinces those who possess discerning minds. For heralds of his will have now been sent out, not professing grammatical art, but displaying his will in simple and guileless words, so that absolutely anyone, upon hearing, understands what is being said, and not with some grudging polish that is unwilling to make itself available to everyone. Yet here you are: besides not understanding what benefits you, you laugh, to your own harm, at the truth that has lived as a citizen among barbarians—to your condemnation. Though it has now visited even you, you do not wish to receive it as a guest, because of your wanton conduct and the plainness of its words, so that you may not be exposed as people who are lovers of words to no purpose and not philosophers who love truth. How long, then, will you keep learning to talk, you who do not know how to speak well? For many utterances from you are not worth one word. What, then, will your Greek multitude say, once it has become one soul, if there is indeed to be a judgment, as this man says? ‘Why, God, did you not proclaim your will to us?’ Will you not surely hear—if indeed you are deemed worthy of an answer—the following? ‘I knew, before the foundation of the world, every choice that would be made, and secretly went beforehand to meet each person according to what that person deserved. But wishing to give those who have taken refuge with me full assurance of this very fact—that it is so, and why I did not allow my will to be proclaimed publicly from the beginning, starting with earlier generations—I have now, near the end of life, sent heralds of my counsel. They are laughed at and, while being insulted, are mocked by people who wish to receive no benefit and who have forcefully rejected my friendship. Oh, the magnitude of the injustice! Heralds risk being murdered, and this at the hands of men who are being called to salvation!’”

lexical_decisions.chosen: as though he were some raving barbarian
lexical_decisions.rationale: δαιμονάω can suggest being possessed or behaving madly. “Raving” preserves the hostile characterization without deciding whether the mockers meant literal possession.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ζήλῳ οὐκ οἶδ’ ὅπως ληφθεὶς εὐσεβεῖ θυμῷ
lexical_decisions.chosen: seized—I do not know how—with zeal and pious indignation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two datival expressions describe Clement’s impelling zeal and religiously framed passion or anger. θυμός could also be rendered “ardor” or “anger.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὡς ἐξ ὧν νῦν τοὺς κριτικὸν νοῦν ἔχοντας πληροφορῶν φαίνεται
lexical_decisions.chosen: as is now evident from the very things by which he fully convinces those who possess discerning minds
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering takes φαίνεται impersonally in English and treats ἐξ ὧν as the evidentiary basis by which God convinces discerning people. Alternatively, the phrase may mean that God’s present convincing of discerning people is itself what makes the hearers’ unworthiness apparent.

lexical_decisions.chosen: not professing grammatical art
lexical_decisions.rationale: γραμματικὴ τέχνη refers to educated literary or grammatical expertise. The relatively literal wording preserves the contrast with the heralds’ simple speech.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐ μετὰ ξέσεώς τινος φθονερᾶς, παρέχειν πᾶσιν ἑαυτὴν μὴ βουλομένης
lexical_decisions.chosen: not with some grudging polish that is unwilling to make itself available to everyone
lexical_decisions.rationale: ξέσις is literally a scraping or polishing and here depicts refined rhetorical finish. The feminine participle most directly agrees with ξέσεως, personifying such refinement as grudgingly inaccessible; it could alternatively be understood more broadly of an elitist mode of presentation.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν εἰς τὴν ὑμετέραν καταδίκην ἐν βαρβάροις πολιτευσαμένην ἀλήθειαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the truth that has lived as a citizen among barbarians—to your condemnation
lexical_decisions.rationale: πολιτεύομαι carries civic imagery: truth has conducted its life or held citizenship among those the Greeks call barbarians. The following ξενίσαι continues the contrasting guest imagery.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰκῇ φιλόλογοί ἐστε καὶ οὐ φιλαληθεῖς φιλόσοφοι
lexical_decisions.chosen: you are lovers of words to no purpose and not philosophers who love truth
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wording preserves the author’s contrast and wordplay between φιλόλογοι, φιλαληθεῖς, and φιλόσοφοι. εἰκῇ marks their devotion to words as vain or purposeless.

lexical_decisions.chosen: Will you not surely hear
lexical_decisions.rationale: In this rhetorical question πάντως is taken affirmatively as “surely” or “certainly.” In a declarative setting οὐ πάντως could instead mean “not altogether” or “not necessarily,” but that reading fits the present question poorly.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάσας τὰς ἐσομένας πρὸ καταβολῆς κόσμου εἰδὼς προαιρέσεις
lexical_decisions.chosen: I knew, before the foundation of the world, every choice that would be made
lexical_decisions.rationale: προαίρεσις can denote a choice, purpose, or moral disposition. “Choice” preserves the emphasis on acts or orientations of volition without adding a developed theory of free will.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦτο δὲ αὐτὸ ὅτι οὕτως ἔχει βουληθεὶς τοὺς προσπεφευγότας μοι πληροφορήσαι διὰ τί
lexical_decisions.chosen: wishing to give those who have taken refuge with me full assurance of this very fact—that it is so, and why
lexical_decisions.rationale: The rendering treats ὅτι οὕτως ἔχει and the following διὰ τί clause as coordinated content of πληροφορήσαι. It is also possible to construe the wording more tightly as assurance precisely about why matters stand this way.

lexical_decisions.chosen: near the end of life
lexical_decisions.rationale: βίος literally denotes life or its course. In this universal historical context it may refer more broadly to the close of the present course of worldly life, but “age” or “world” is not explicitly written.

lexical_decisions.chosen: who have forcefully rejected my friendship
lexical_decisions.rationale: παραιτέομαι means declining, refusing, or rejecting, and ἐπιτεταμένως gives the refusal an emphatic or strenuous character.

passages.text: “‘This injustice being committed against my heralds would have been committed against everyone from the beginning, if the unworthy had been called to salvation from the beginning. For what they now do unjustly serves as a defense of my just providence: I rightly did not wish, from the beginning, to expose publicly to abuse, and to no benefit, the message worthy of honor. Instead, I resolved that it should be kept unspoken as something precious—not withheld from those who were worthy from the beginning, for I did share it with them, but from these people and others like them, who, as you see, are unworthy, who hate me and do not wish to love themselves.’ And now, at any rate, stop laughing at this man. Question me about his proclamation, or let anyone who wishes answer me when I question him. Do not bark like wanton dogs, shutting the ears of those who wish to be saved with disorderly noise. You unjust people, hateful to God and turning the reasoning that saves aside into unbelief, how can you obtain pardon when you insult the man who offers to tell you about God’s divine nature—and that too a man whom you ought to have welcomed because of his good intention toward you, even if he said nothing true?”

lexical_decisions.chosen: the message worthy of honor
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγος here is the proclaimed teaching or message rather than merely an individual word. “The discourse worthy of honor” is also possible.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to expose publicly to abuse
lexical_decisions.rationale: The literal construction is to “place” the message publicly into insult or outrage. “Expose publicly to abuse” conveys both the placement and its intended result.

lexical_decisions.chosen: it should be kept unspoken as something precious
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive σιγᾶσθαι means that the message is to be kept silent or left unspoken, while τίμιον can mean precious, highly valued, or honorable.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὐκ ἀπὸ τῶν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς ἀξίων (οἷς καὶ μετέδωκα), ἀλλὰ ἀπὸ τούτων καὶ τῶν τοιούτων
lexical_decisions.chosen: not withheld from those who were worthy from the beginning, for I did share it with them, but from these people and others like them
lexical_decisions.rationale: The repeated ἀπό depends on the idea of being kept unspoken from particular groups. “Withheld” makes that relation idiomatic without supplying any missing content.

lexical_decisions.chosen: about his proclamation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπάγγελμα can mean a declaration, profession, undertaking, claim, or promise. Here it denotes what Barnabas publicly professes or proclaims; “about his claim” is a viable alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: bark like wanton dogs
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀσελγής may mean wanton, shameless, insolent, or undisciplined. “Wanton” preserves the severity of the insult without narrowing it to sexual misconduct.

lexical_decisions.chosen: hateful to God
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compound most naturally has a passive sense, “hated by” or “hateful to God,” and commonly characterizes the impious. “God-hating” is lexically possible if the compound is taken actively.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸν σώζοντα λογισμὸν εἰς ἀπιστίαν ἀπασχολοῦντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: turning the reasoning that saves aside into unbelief
lexical_decisions.rationale: λογισμός is reasoning, reflection, or the rational faculty, and ἀπασχολέω describes diverting or preoccupying it. The phrase depicts their noise as redirecting potentially saving thought toward unbelief.

lexical_decisions.chosen: God’s divine nature
lexical_decisions.rationale: θειότης denotes divinity or divine nature. The rendering retains the source’s explicit genitive “of God” rather than replacing it with a different theological formulation.

source_issues.source_quote: καὶ νῦν γε παρέντες· γελᾶν τὸν ἄνδρα τοῦτον ἐμοῦ πρὸς τὸ τούτου ἐπάγγελμα πυνθάνεσθε
source_issues.issue: The printed middle point after παρέντες separates the participle from the infinitive γελᾶν, although παρέντες γελᾶν gives the defensible sense “stop laughing.” The translation treats the punctuation as editorial and construes ἐμοῦ with πυνθάνεσθε, “question me.” No wording is supplied or removed.

## Theological stance

The People's Open Bible does not commit to a specific denominational
or creedal doctrinal stance. Where the source texts presuppose
theological claims — the divinity of Christ, the resurrection,
the personhood of the Holy Spirit, the unity of God — the
translation reflects those claims as the texts present them, not
as imposed commitments of the translator.

Readers from any tradition (Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Protestant
of any stripe, non-denominational, inquirer) are invited to
evaluate POB against their own framework. Where a translation
decision is influenced by a theological reading — for example,
where a Greek construction is genuinely ambiguous and the English
choice leans one way or the other — that choice is documented in
the verse's `theological_decisions` block and the alternative
rendering is preserved in a footnote.

We do not pick sides on denominational distinctives (Reformed vs.
Arminian, infant vs. believer's baptism, real presence vs.
symbolic, cessationist vs. continuationist, etc.). Those questions
are for the reader and their faith community, not for the
translation.

## Translation philosophy

The People's Open Bible aims at **optimal equivalence**: the most faithful,
intelligible English representation of the source's meaning, wording patterns,
literary form, and rhetorical force. This is not an automatic midpoint between
formal and dynamic translation. Readability serves source fidelity; convention
and familiarity do not override it.

Specifically:

1. **Original-language primacy with reader-conscious wording.** Where
   long-standing English renderings obscure the source text's plain
   sense, we explain the source pressure openly. For *doulos*, the main
   text uses "servant" consistently while notes and the public audit
   trail preserve bonded-status, ownership, and total-allegiance nuance
   where it is historically or theologically salient (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1).

2. **Translate titles; use conventional name forms.** Christological
   titles are translated to preserve meaning (*Christos* →
   "Messiah" when it functions independently as a title; *Kyrios* →
   "Lord"). In name-like constructions, use the familiar English forms
   "Jesus Christ" and "Christ Jesus." Personal names are otherwise
   transliterated by standard conventions. Thus "Jesus is the Messiah"
   retains the title, while Greek *Iēsous Christos* used as a personal-name
   construction is rendered "Jesus Christ."

3. **Preserve theological tension rather than resolve it.** Where
   the source is genuinely ambiguous on a contested interpretive
   question (e.g., *pistis Christou* — "faith in Christ" vs.
   "faithfulness of Christ"), we render one in the main text and
   preserve the alternative in a footnote, documenting the
   decision in the per-verse YAML.

4. **Consistency of key terms, or documented exception.** A given
   Greek or Hebrew word should receive a consistent English gloss
   across the translation, unless context demands variance — in
   which case the variance is documented per-verse with a
   rationale. The `consistency_lint.py` tool enforces this at
   commit time.

5. **Readable modern English, not archaic or academic.** The
   target reader is a literate 18–35-year-old English speaker.
   Vocabulary should be accessible without flattening theological
   weight. We avoid both ecclesiastical jargon ("propitiation" is
   footnoted, not required) and informality that undersells the
   text's gravity.

## Source distinctions and optimal English

Source fidelity takes priority over mere familiarity or defensibility. A
significant Greek or Hebrew wording pattern must receive an explicit comparison
with the best source-transparent English candidate, even when a prior draft
already discusses it in a footnote. Prior rationale is evidence, not a veto.
Do not infer different meanings from morphology alone or invent theology to
justify different glosses; preserve observable wording without adding claims.
A concise source-qualified or hyphenated rendering is available when ordinary
English otherwise conceals the source pattern. Record unresolved proposals for
maintainer review; do not silently certify them as unchanged or auto-publish.

**Approved scoped rendering:** John 21:15–17 uses **agape-love** for ἀγαπάω

## Reorientation terminology (2026-10-11)

Maintainer-approved English POB and SPOB reader wording uses **reorient /
reorientation** in place of the repent family for moral-spiritual redirection.
Use **toward God** when the context warrants making that direction explicit;
use **toward you** in direct prayer, and omit the extra destination when the
sentence already names it, supplies a departure from wrongdoing, or concerns
interpersonal reconsideration. Acts 20:21 explicitly supplies the Godward
phrase. The word *metanoia* by itself does not lexically contain "God."

This is an English editorial policy, not a claim that remorse is irrelevant or
that Greek word parts establish the full meaning. Preserve sorrow, named sins,
faith, forgiveness, and the distinction between a response and its fruit.
Keep separate turning expressions in Acts 3:19 and 26:20. Baptism's relationship
to reorientation must not be rewritten as "only symbolizes" or "causes."

**Context controls exceptions.** Retain regret, relenting, reconsideration,
change of mind, or turning back where that is the supported sense. Do not make
God reorient toward God; do not make a persecutor's demand for apostasy a call
toward God. Preserve contested interpretations in Job 42:6 and Hebrews 12:17.
Extra-canonical authors retain their own conceptual frameworks. Adapting a
historical English witness is not a new ancient-language translation, and must
be disclosed while its source transcription remains untouched.

**No invented intensifiers.** Do not add "fully," "completely," "radically,"
"truly," "wholeheartedly," or a superlative simply to strengthen reorientation.
Preserve such force only where the source supplies it. Hermas V.3.xiii.4
(reader chapter 21:4) has *holotelōs* and *ex holēs kardias*; its existing
"completely" and "from their whole heart" are not new additions.

Traditional terminology remains in alternative notes, original sources, and
historical revision records. Do not rewrite those layers to manufacture a
history of agreement. See [the application report](docs/REORIENTATION_POLICY_2026-10-11.md)
and the hash-bound plan in `config/terminology/`.

## What the translation is not

To prevent misunderstanding:

- **Not a paraphrase.** Every English rendering is tied to a
  specific source-text word or phrase, documented in the per-verse
  YAML.
- **Not a study Bible.** Footnotes document translation decisions,
  not doctrinal application or devotional commentary.
- **Not a denominational product.** The translation is
  intentionally cross-denominational. Contested readings are
  preserved in footnotes, not smoothed away.
- **Not a finalized translation.** Every verse is currently an
  AI-drafted rendering, released openly with full rationale. There
  is no formal scholarly review process at this time.
- **Not a first-century English approximation.** We aim at modern
  English that honors source-language meaning, not at archaism.

## Translating into other languages

The People's Open Bible's long-term intention is to be translated
into every major world language. Scripture belongs to the whole
church; producing POB only in English would contradict the
project's mission.

Each target language is its own translation — drafted directly
from the original-language sources (Hebrew OT, Greek NT, Swete
LXX for the deuterocanonical books) rather than from the English
POB. Translating from English would compound the distance from the
originals and inherit choices that make sense in English but not
elsewhere. Every target language deserves its own encounter with
the Hebrew and Greek.

Each language goes through **several revision passes** before it
is considered stable:

1. **AI-drafted first pass** — a frontier multilingual model
   produces the initial verse-by-verse draft with full per-verse
   provenance, following the same methodology used for English
   (DOCTRINE.md translation philosophy §§1–5, per-verse YAML
   schema, `doctrine_reference` citations where relevant).
2. **AI-reviewer revision** — a second, distinct model reads the
   draft and flags awkward phrasing, dropped nuance, or places
   where the target language's idiom has drifted from the
   source's force. Revisions are discrete commits.
3. **Native-speaker community review** — before a language is
   declared stable, speakers of that language who are also
   familiar with the biblical source languages (or who have
   access to published lexicons in that language) audit the
   text and raise issues publicly.
4. **Public issue window** — a minimum public-review period with
   open GitHub issues before any language moves from "preview"
   to "stable."

**Supported languages will be disclosed publicly based on model
performance and feasibility.** Not every language has an AI model
capable of scholarly-accurate translation yet, and not every
language has a sufficient community of native-speaking reviewers
accessible to the project. We will publish the current supported-
language list, and the ready-but-not-yet-stable list, as we reach
the capability threshold for each. Languages that do not yet meet
the bar are named as such, not silently omitted.

Every language published under this program carries the same
CC-BY 4.0 license, the same per-verse provenance, the same
auditability. There is no tier system across languages — every
supported language gets the full People's Open Bible.
